Before you start

Students find their default conflict style, write a soft, specific first sentence for a roommate problem, and learn when a roommate problem becomes a safety call. Bring index cards, and take the Dev and Luke card slowly: it's about a roommate who may be suicidal.

Every student in the room

On the Sofia and Hannah card, say plainly that neither the nightly family call nor the quiet bedtime is wrong; families teach different rules about noise, privacy and speaking up.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn why the roommate relationship matters, recognize their own default conflict style and where it came from, practice a soft, specific opening line (notice, effect, ask), and know when a roommate problem is really a safety problem.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per student
  • The five conflict styles on the board or slide
  • The student page link (last slide) to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minCan a roommate change your grades? (guess)
  2. 3 minFive conflict styles: stand by your default; house rules travel
  3. 6 minStart soft and specific: write a first sentence, read it, share
  4. 5 minTwo rooms: Sofia and Hannah, Dev and Luke
  5. 3 minEvery student, the big five, close

Short on time (10-minute version)

Five conflict styles (3), notice, effect, ask (4), Dev and Luke only (3).

Before you teach
Steer away from who's right.

In the Sofia and Hannah story, both habits are reasonable. If the room starts judging Sofia's family or Hannah's quiet, bring it back to the question: what would a collaborating version sound like?

Dev and Luke's story is about suicide risk.

Read it slowly. Say clearly that a roommate who "doesn't see the point" is a safety situation, that telling an RA is the right call, and that asking directly about suicide doesn't put the idea in anyone's head.

Some students won't have a roommate.

Commuters, students living at home, gap-year students and students headed to work or the military are in the room too. The conflict skills work with siblings, coworkers and teammates. Say so.

Don't ask about home.

"How did your family handle disagreements?" is a private reflection, not a share-out. Some homes handled conflict with yelling, silence or worse.

Identity isn't a conflict style.

If a student raises a roommate's race, religion, sexuality, gender identity or disability as a "problem," be clear: slurs and mocking aren't a style difference, and colleges have bias reporting for that.

After the lesson.

If a student tells you they're worried about a friend or about themselves, follow up one on one that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

House rules travel.

In some families you say what bothers you and it's over in five minutes; in others a direct complaint is rude, and people hint or go through someone else. Present both as learned rules, never as better and worse.

Faith and values in a shared room.

One roommate may pray five times a day, another may never have been religious; one may drink and the other not. Name values as one of the big five to discuss, not a reason to avoid each other.

Shared rooms aren't new to everyone.

Some students have always shared a room with siblings; others have never shared. Neither is the default.

Race and difference.

The Shook and Fazio study shows white students with a Black roommate reported less satisfaction early on, and less anxiety and better attitudes by the end of the term. Present it as a reason to give a roommate who's different from you time, never as a comment on any student.

LGBTQ+ students.

Some students worry about how a roommate will react to who they are. Housing offices and RAs can help with roommate matching and room changes. Say that out loud.

Disability and neurodivergence.

Sensory needs, medical equipment, sleep schedules and medication can all be part of a roommate agreement. Disability services can help with housing accommodations.

What the research says

Dartmouth assigns first-year roommates at random. Students' grades moved with their roommates' grades, and roommates influenced whether each other joined fraternities.

Sacerdote, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2001

At another school with random assignment, men placed with a roommate who drank often before college ended up with GPAs about a quarter point lower. Women's grades weren't affected.

Kremer and Levy, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2008

A review ties the quality of the roommate relationship to adjustment to college and to mental health.

Erb, Renshaw, Short and Pollard, Journal of Student Affairs Research and Practice, 2014

Among randomly assigned first-years, white students living with a Black roommate reported less satisfaction early on, and by the end of the term their anxiety about interacting across race had dropped and their attitudes had improved.

Shook and Fazio, Psychological Science, 2008

In 124 newlywed couples, how the first three minutes of a disagreement went predicted which couples would divorce over six years. Opening with criticism of the person, instead of a specific complaint, did worse.

Carrère and Gottman, Family Process, 1999

The Thomas-Kilmann model maps five conflict styles (competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating). Each fits some situations; most people have a default.

Thomas and Kilmann, 1974
